<idea>Implement the Erdős–Soifer family directly: for each k, start from the k×k grid of cells of side 1/k and replace one m×m block of cells by an (m+1)×(m+1) grid of squares of side m/((m+1)k). This adds 2m+1 squares and m/k to the total, so n = k²+2m+1 gives k + m/k. Evaluate every feasible (k, m) for the given n, pad any surplus with size-zero squares, and keep the best.</idea>

<idea>Add the shrinking variant to the same search: replace an (m+1)×(m+1) block of cells by an m×m grid of squares of side (m+1)/(mk). This removes 2m+1 squares at a cost of (m+1)/k, so a larger k can be used when n sits just below a perfect square (e.g. n=6, 8, 11, 13, 15). Take the maximum over both variants and all k.</idea>

<idea>Generalise to multiple disjoint block replacements inside one k×k grid, with different block sizes and either direction. Solve a small knapsack over (count change, sum change) pairs to hit exactly n squares with maximal total, padding with zero squares only if needed.</idea>

<idea>Allow the replaced block to be a rectangle: an a×b block of cells, re-tiled by p×q equal squares of side min(a/p, b/q)/k. Enumerate all small a, b, p, q to find count/sum trade-offs the square-block construction misses. This matters especially for even n, where single square-block changes only shift the count by odd amounts.</idea>

<idea>Use non-uniform grids: choose row heights h_i and column widths w_j and put a square of side min(h_i, w_j) in each cell. Optimise these sizes with an LP or SLSQP, together with subdivided cells, to maximise the sum for awkward n. Seed the optimisation from the best Erdős–Soifer configuration.</idea>

<idea>Recursive guillotine dynamic programming: f(rectangle a×b, count n) = best of placing a single square or making a vertical/horizontal cut and splitting n between the parts. Run it over a discretised set of rectangle dimensions, e.g. multiples of 1/(k·L), to discover axis-aligned packings better than the formula.</idea>

<idea>Build the configuration from a staircase/L-shaped strip: keep a (k−1)×(k−1) grid of side 1/k in one corner. Fill the remaining L-shaped strip of width 1/k with squares of side 1/(k+j) or smaller, chosen so the count and sum work out; this gives intermediate n values between the block-replacement constructions.</idea>

<idea>As a long shot for rotated squares, place 45°-rotated small squares into gaps left by an axis-aligned grid whose cells are slightly shrunk. Use penalty-based gradient optimisation (separating-axis overlap penalty plus containment penalty) to maximise the sum, starting from the best constructive answer.</idea>

<idea>Add a robust validation-and-shrink step: compute exact coordinates with rationals or Fractions, then scale every side by (1−1e-12) about its centre. This ensures no floating-point overlap or out-of-bounds error loses points in the evaluator, while costing a negligible amount of score.</idea>

<idea>Run a fast local search over discrete configurations (grid parameter k, block positions and sizes, and which squares to merge or split) using a simulated-annealing loop for a few seconds. Score each candidate with the exact sum-of-sides formula and return the best valid packing found.</idea>

<idea>Safe baseline fix: for each n, also try k = ceil(sqrt(n)) and use n cells of the k×k grid with side 1/k, giving n/k. This alone matches the best known values for n=8 and n=15. Return the maximum of this and every other construction found.</idea>

<idea>Represent axis-aligned packings as sequence pairs, which fix for each pair of squares whether one is left of or below the other. For a fixed sequence pair, maximise the sum of sides with an exact LP whose variables are the positions and sides, using linear separation and containment constraints. Search over sequence pairs with simulated annealing, seeded from the best grid-based construction, until the time budget runs out.</idea>

<idea>Exact tiling search on an integer L×L board for L up to about 10–12. Use a broken-profile (skyline) DP or exact-cover backtracking to enumerate dissections of the board into integer squares, recording the best total of sides per count. Scale by 1/L, and pad or drop cells (as zero squares) to hit n exactly.</idea>

<idea>Use an ILP or set-partitioning solver, such as scipy milp, on a k×k cell grid. Each candidate is an a×a axis-aligned block at any position, chosen with a binary variable; constraints are that each cell is covered at most once and that the number of squares chosen equals n. Maximise the sum of a/k, and loop over k from about sqrt(n)−2 to 2·sqrt(n).</idea>

<idea>Dynamic program over multisets of square sizes. Moves are splitting a square of side s into j×j squares of side s/j (adding j²−1 squares and gaining (j−1)s), or merging an aligned j×j group back into one. Run best-first search from every k×k grid to fill a table best[n] and its realising layout, keeping the geometry as an explicit quadtree-like tree.</idea>

<idea>Column-strip construction: split the unit square into vertical strips of widths w_i, and stack c_i equal squares of side min(w_i, 1/c_i) in each strip. Each strip may also be recursively split horizontally into sub-strips. Optimise the integers c_i by DP, setting the widths to w_i = 1/c_i where possible and giving any leftover width to a final strip, to cover counts the square-grid families miss.</idea>

<idea>Two-scale mixed lattice: tile the square with a p×p grid in which some cells hold one square of side 1/p and others hold a q×q subgrid. Allow p and q to be coprime-unrelated, and let the subdivided region be a whole band of rows so that the band is re-gridded with a different column count. Enumerate p, q, the band heights and counts in closed form.</idea>

<idea>Gap-filling post-processor: after any construction, compute the free space as a union of axis-aligned empty rectangles, using maximal-rectangle enumeration. Repeatedly replace a zero-size padding square with the largest square that fits a free rectangle, and enlarge existing squares into adjacent slack using an LP over sides with positions free.</idea>

<idea>Tilted-band long shot: lay out the k×k grid but replace one row (or column) with k+1 squares rotated by a small angle θ, stacked as a tilted chain in a strip of height slightly above 1/k. Shrink the other rows accordingly, then optimise θ, the strip height and the side lengths numerically with exact separating-axis feasibility checks. This targets n = k²+1-type values where a lattice cannot fit the extra square.</idea>

<idea>Recursive “one big square plus two rectangles” construction: put a square of side s in a corner and split the remaining L-shape into two rectangles. Fill each rectangle optimally by a memoised recursion on (aspect ratio, count), where a rectangle a×b with count m is filled by a grid of ⌊b/a⌋-style columns or recursion. Optimise s over a fine set of rationals.</idea>

<idea>Substitution DP: any square of side s in a packing can be replaced by a scaled copy of a packing of m squares, so f(n+m−1) ≥ f(n) − s + s·f(m). Fill a table best[n] bottom-up from the k×k grids, keeping each layout as an explicit tree. At each step substitute into either the largest or the smallest square, and try every m that has already been solved.</idea>

<idea>Over-build then delete: build Erdős–Soifer or grid configurations for every N in n..n+2√n+2 and delete the N−n smallest squares. This gives f(n) ≥ f(N) − (sum of the N−n smallest sides). Add every such candidate to the pool and keep the best one that is valid.</idea>

<idea>Multiset-first packing: enumerate multisets of sides from {1/d} (d up to about 3√n) by a knapsack. Maximise the sum subject to the count being n and the area being at most 1, then test the top candidates for exact packability. The test is a bottom-left/skyline backtracking search on the integer board of size lcm(d's) × lcm(d's), returning the first multiset that packs.</idea>

<idea>Exact axis-aligned optimum for small n via a big-M MILP in scipy.optimize.milp. Use continuous centres and sides, and four binary separation indicators per pair (left/right/below/above, at least one active). Add symmetry breaking (sort by side, put the first square in the bottom-left quadrant) and warm-start from the best construction.</idea>

<idea>Inflation multi-start for rotated packings: start from many random centres, angles and tiny sides. Run a Lubachevsky–Stillinger-style growth in which each square's side grows at a rate proportional to its slack. Resolve overlaps with separating-axis push-apart moves plus rotation, then run a final SLSQP polish on sum(sides) with exact separating-axis constraints.</idea>

<idea>Symmetry-constrained continuous search: impose mirror or 180°-rotational symmetry (with an odd central square when n is odd). This halves the variables in the penalty/SLSQP optimisation of rotated squares and lets many more restarts fit in 60 s, exploring structures such as a central tilted square surrounded by symmetric axis-aligned rings.</idea>

<idea>Pythagorean-tiling candidate: tile the plane with two square sizes a and b in the Pythagorean (pinwheel) arrangement, optionally rotated by a small angle. Clip it to the unit square, keeping only squares that lie fully inside and zero-padding. Optimise a, b, the offset and the angle numerically to see whether the two-size lattice beats grid families for some n.</idea>

<idea>Beam-search greedy placement: compute the largest empty axis-aligned square in the current free region (L∞-Voronoi / maximal empty square). At each step choose among a few candidate sizes at the top candidate positions, scoring partial states by sum + (remaining count)·(average feasible future side). Keep a beam of 50–200 states.</idea>

<idea>Tilted-lattice core with axis-aligned border: place a k×k block of squares rotated by a Pythagorean angle such as atan(1/2) or atan(3/4) in the middle. Fill the four triangular-ish border regions with axis-aligned small squares from the guillotine/strip routines. Optimise the lattice side and angle so the total count is n, as a long shot for n just above a perfect square.</idea>

<idea>Nested two-level Erdős–Soifer closed form: inside the (m+1)×(m+1) replacement grid, apply a second replacement of an m2×m2 block by (m2±1)² squares. This gives counts k² + 2m+1 ± (2m2±1) with explicit sums. Enumerate all (k, m, m2, signs, positions) and take the best that exactly matches n.</idea>

<idea>Ring recursion: surround a central square of side 1−2a with a frame of 4(j−1) squares of side a=1/j along all four edges. Fill the central square recursively with the best scaled packing for the remaining count, and enumerate j and the recursion depth. One-sided L-frames already give n=6 (7/3) and n=11 (3/4 frame of 7 plus four squares of 3/8, totalling 3.25), and this generalises them to two- and four-sided frames.</idea>

<idea>Exact rectangle table g(p,q,m): for integer rectangles p×q up to about 12 and counts m up to n, store the best sum from a single square, a uniform grid, or one guillotine cut. Compute it with memoised DP in exact Fractions. The unit square is then filled by trying every split of the 1×1 board at rational cut positions with denominators up to 12, which captures nested L-shapes and asymmetric cuts in one table.</idea>

<idea>Hole-punch post-optimiser: take the best construction, pick the r smallest squares (r=1..4), delete them, and compute every maximal empty axis-aligned rectangle of the freed region. Refill it with the best g(rectangle, r') packing from the rectangle table, keeping the result if it beats the original at the same count n.</idea>

<idea>Compaction LP on the topology of the best construction: freeze only the left/right/above/below contact relations between squares. Solve an LP maximising the sum of sides under those relations and containment; this often lets unequal neighbours rebalance, for example growing a big corner square while shrinking a strip. Accept the result only if it is strictly larger.</idea>

<idea>Two-band construction with unequal frame widths: give the bottom band height a with ⌊1/a⌋ squares and the left band width b with ⌊(1−a)/b⌋ squares, where a and b are independent unit fractions. Fill the remaining (1−b)×(1−a) rectangle with the best grid of near-square cells. Enumerate a and b over 1/2..1/(2√n) and the inner grid shape, in closed form.</idea>

<idea>Geometric staircase along the diagonal: place squares of decreasing sides s1>s2>… along the main diagonal. Fill the two triangular-ish complementary staircase regions with column and row stacks whose sizes are matched to the step heights. Optimise the s_i with SLSQP for each n as a structurally different, non-grid family.</idea>

<idea>Upper-bound-pruned exhaustive search for small n (≤20): enumerate axis-aligned dissections in bottom-left skyline order with side choices from {i/L : L≤12}. Prune with the Cauchy–Schwarz bound sum ≤ current + √(m·remaining area) and with the best known lower bound, so the exact discrete optimum is found within the time limit.</idea>

<idea>Rotated-insert perturbation: in the best axis-aligned configuration, find pairs of adjacent equal squares in a strip whose width has slack, and replace a run of t squares by t+1 squares tilted at angle θ. Solve the 1-D chain-in-strip problem (side as a function of θ and strip width) in closed form and accept the change when the count-adjusted sum improves.</idea>

<idea>Count-parity fix via 2×1 dominos: replace a 1×2 block of cells of side 1/k by three squares (one of side 1/k... rather two of side 1/(2k) stacked plus one of 1/k), or 2×3 blocks by six cells' worth of mixed sizes. Tabulate every small rectangular block retiling with (Δcount, Δsum) from the exact rectangle table, then knapsack these onto disjoint regions of the k×k grid to hit even n exactly.</idea>

<idea>Safety-first output: build every candidate in exact Fractions, validate it with an exact axis-aligned overlap and containment checker (separating axis with an epsilon for any rotated ones), and shrink sides by 1e-12 only if needed. If the top candidate fails, fall back to the next valid candidate, so no n ever scores below the plain ceil(√n) grid value n/⌈√n⌉.</idea>

<idea>Add a partition recurrence: split the unit square into a j×j grid of equal sub-squares (j=2,3,4) and give each sub-square its own count n_i with Σn_i = n. This gives f(n) ≥ (1/j)·max Σ f(n_i), computed by a knapsack over a best[] table built bottom-up. Unlike single-square substitution, the extra count is spread over all cells, which reaches mixed-parity counts.</idea>

<idea>Generate perfect and imperfect squared rectangles via Brooks–Smith–Stone–Tutte electrical networks. Enumerate small planar graphs (up to about n+3 edges), solve Kirchhoff's equations exactly with Fractions to get square dissections of a square with exactly n tiles, and take the best sum. Near-square rectangle dissections are also kept, scaled into the unit square with the leftover strip filled by zero-size or small squares.</idea>

<idea>Use a genetic/decoder approach. A chromosome is an ordered list of n sides drawn from {1/d}, and a deterministic skyline (bottom-left-fill) decoder places them and sets any square that does not fit to zero. Evolve multisets and orderings with crossover and mutation for ~40 s, seeded from the grid and Erdős–Soifer multisets.</idea>

<idea>Use non-guillotine pinwheel decompositions. Split the unit square into four rectangles spiralling around a central rectangle, with the cut positions enumerated over rationals of denominator ≤ 12. Fill each of the five rectangles from an exact rectangle-count table, which captures layouts no sequence of straight cuts can reach.</idea>

<idea>Compute a global table best[m] with its layouts once per process, for all m up to max(n) + 2√n, stored in a module-level cache. Every construction family (grids, replacements, partitions, substitutions) can then feed the others, and repeated calls cost nothing. This leaves most of the 60 s budget for numerical refinement of only the current n.</idea>

<idea>Implement the known upper bounds as an early exit and a search guide. These are f(k²) = k (Erdős), the bound f(k²+1) ≤ k for k ≤ 13 (Halbeisen), and the Cauchy–Schwarz bound √n. When a candidate meets the bound, return immediately; otherwise spend the remaining time on the n with the largest gap between candidate and bound.</idea>

<idea>Seam construction with tilted squares: put a k-column grid on the left part of the square and a (k+1)-column grid on the right, with different row pitches. Along the vertical seam where the pitches mismatch, insert a column of slightly rotated squares. Optimise the seam position, the angles and the sides with SLSQP using exact separating-axis constraints, so that counts between the two lattices fill naturally.</idea>

<idea>Column generation for strip-based packings. Each column pattern is a vertical strip of width w holding a mixed stack, such as one square of side w plus pairs of side w/2 side by side. Solve the master LP "choose strips with total width ≤ 1 and exact count n, maximising the sum", price new strip patterns by DP, then round to integers.</idea>

<idea>Shift-and-squeeze brick rows: lay out rows of equal squares in which consecutive rows are offset by half a cell. Shrink a few rows so that one row can host an extra square of a different size in the freed gap. Optimise the row heights and offsets by LP for fixed integer row counts, enumerating row-count vectors whose total is n.</idea>

<idea>Large-neighbourhood search on the best axis-aligned layout. Repeatedly free a random window (for example a 2×2 to 4×4 region of cells), then solve the window exactly. The exact solve maximises the sum of sides inside the window's bounding box with a fixed count, using the small big-M MILP or a brute-force integer tiling. Accept improvements and cycle through windows and counts until the time limit.</idea>

<idea>Continuous two-rectangle split: cut the unit square at height t into a 1×t and a 1×(1−t) rectangle and fill each with a uniform p×q (resp. p'×q') grid of side min(t/p, 1/q) (resp. min((1−t)/p', 1/q')). For every integer tuple with pq+p'q' ≥ n, solve analytically for the optimal t (a breakpoint of piecewise-linear functions), then recurse one level on the larger part.</idea>

<idea>Euclidean-algorithm squared rectangles: for a rational aspect a/b, greedily cut the largest possible square from the remaining rectangle (the continued-fraction dissection). Place such a rectangle in the unit square, fill the complementary strip with a grid, and subdivide individual pieces into j×j grids. Enumerate a/b with small denominators to hit count n with the maximal sum.</idea>

<idea>Use OR-Tools CP-SAT, if importable, with optional 2D intervals (AddNoOverlap2D) on an integer L×L board. Each candidate square has a size variable chosen from a domain, presence literals are constrained to sum to n, and the objective is the total of the sides. Iterate L over 6..16 with time slices and fall back to the closed-form constructions if the library is absent.</idea>

<idea>Three-level nested shelves: rows inside columns inside rows. Each shelf has an integer count c, and its height equals the shelf's square side. Shelves stack until the leftover, which is filled by a transposed shelf system, recursively to depth 3. Enumerate the count vectors by DP over the remaining (width, height, count) state, using exact Fractions.</idea>

<idea>Size-class realisability search: fix 2–3 size classes with counts (n1, n2, n3) and sides (s1, s2, s3) tied by small integer ratios. Maximise Σ n_i s_i subject to the area constraint and a strip-packing necessary condition: the number of columns of the largest class times s1 must be ≤ 1. Then construct the layout explicitly by placing the big class as a corner block and greedily tiling the L-shaped remainder with the smaller classes.</idea>

<idea>Pattern mining from the best-known values: all listed optima have the form (k² + a)/k or (k·j + b)/j with small integers. Generate every rational of this form near √n, and for each target rebuild a matching layout by bounded backtracking on the corresponding k×k or j×j integer board. A target therefore steers an exact search instead of blind enumeration.</idea>

<idea>Two-orientation hybrid in one block: replace an m×m block of cells by a 45°-rotated grid of diamonds of side s. Fill the four corner triangles of that block with axis-aligned staircases of tiny squares. Choose s and the diamond count analytically so the block gains count at a sum cost below the Erdős–Soifer replacement's, then insert the block via the existing knapsack.</idea>

<idea>Parallel portfolio: run independent construction families (closed forms, guillotine DP, MILP/CP, continuous rotated optimisation) in separate multiprocessing workers with hard deadlines of about 50 s. A shared best-so-far value prunes all of them. The parent validates and returns the best certified packing, so slow exact searches never risk the time limit.</idea>

<idea>Contact-graph flipping search: represent the axis-aligned packing by its horizontal and vertical constraint graphs. Make local moves that flip one adjacency (left-of becomes below-of) or merge or split a node, re-solving the sum-maximising LP after each move with warm-started dual simplex. This is a cheaper neighbourhood than full sequence pairs and lets tabu search explore thousands of topologies per second.</idea>

<idea>Asymmetric corner-merge family: in a k×k grid, merge an a×a block in one corner and a b×b block in the opposite corner (with a ≠ b allowed). Also split c cells into 2×2, giving count k² − a² − b² + 2 + 3c and sum k + (a + b − a² − b² + c)/k... wait, corrected: (k² − a² − b² + a + b + c)/k. Enumerate all (k, a, b, c) in closed form to cover even and odd residues near n that single-block replacements miss.</idea>

<idea>Solve a maximum-weight independent set ILP on a mixed-denominator lattice. Candidate axis-aligned squares have sides i/L and corners on an L×L board with highly composite L (12, 24 or 60), so sizes like 1/3, 1/4 and 3/8 coexist. Non-overlap is enforced by a clique constraint at every interior lattice point, plus an exact count of n.</idea>

<idea>Run Monte Carlo Tree Search over bottom-left skyline placements. Each move picks the side of the next square at the lowest-leftmost skyline corner from a small set of rational sizes, and rollouts finish greedily, with the remaining squares counted at their best feasible equal size. Use UCT statistics shared through a transposition table keyed on the skyline profile.</idea>

<idea>Use objective continuation in the continuous optimiser: maximise Σ s_i^p, starting at p=2, where many equal-area tilings are optimal and the landscape is flat. Gradually anneal p down to 1 while keeping the separating-axis and containment constraints, so the optimiser is led from tiling-like configurations towards sum-of-sides optima, possibly rotated ones.</idea>

<idea>Run an L∞ power-diagram (Laguerre–Chebyshev) Lloyd relaxation. Give each of the n sites a weight, compute the L∞ power cells in the unit square, and set each square to the largest axis-aligned square centred in its cell. Iterate moving sites to the cell's Chebyshev centre and rebalancing weights towards equal-side growth.</idea>

<idea>Evolve construction expressions with grammar-based genetic programming. The primitives are grid(p,q), cut(h|v, t, A, B), split(j), merge(j) and ring(j, A), applied to a rectangle. Expressions are evaluated exactly in Fractions to get (count, sum), and the fitness is the best sum at exactly n with zero-padding, so new compositional families are discovered automatically.</idea>

<idea>Build a sheared staircase grid. Shift row i of a k×k-style grid horizontally by i·δ, which opens a staircase of left-edge gaps of widths δ, 2δ, …. Fill those gaps with squares of side iδ (or stacks of smaller ones), shrinking the row squares by LP, and enumerate k and rational δ in closed form to obtain extra counts at small sum cost.</idea>

<idea>Use LP dual sensitivity to guide splitting. Solve the compaction LP for the current best layout, read the dual prices of the containment and adjacency constraints, and split, merge or delete the squares with the most favourable marginal value per unit count change. Re-solve after each edit, which gives a targeted descent across counts n±1, n±3 instead of random moves.</idea>

<idea>Filter knapsack-generated multisets with necessary cumulative-capacity conditions before running the expensive packability tests. The number of squares with side > 1/j is at most (j−1)², and the total side of squares exceeding 1/2 in any row band is at most 1. Also apply an area bound per size threshold, so only plausible multisets reach exact packing.</idea>

<idea>Use tilted equal-square packings as sub-blocks. Precompute, by penalty optimisation, small near-optimal rotated packings of m equal squares in a square container (Friedman-type, e.g. m=5, 10, 11). Treat each as a substitutable block with its (count, scaled sum) in the substitution and partition recurrences, so rotated structures can appear inside otherwise axis-aligned layouts.</idea>

<idea>Use row-slide insertion moves. In the best layout, find a maximal straight line of edges spanning the square (a guillotine seam) and slide everything on one side by δ to open a strip. Fill the strip with a column of equal small squares, then re-solve the compaction LP so neighbours absorb the loss. Choose δ analytically as the breakpoint where the added count's sum exceeds the shrinkage cost.</idea>

<idea>Lagrangian count pricing: for a range of prices λ, maximise (sum of sides − λ·count) over guillotine/grid-tree layouts with a DP that never fixes the count. Each λ yields a layout on the upper convex hull of (count, sum). Then repair the count to exactly n with the cheapest local split, merge or delete, which finds good counts without enumerating every count.</idea>

<idea>Monotone-staircase DP: on an L×L integer board, restrict layouts to those built by placing squares into the inner corners of a Young-diagram-shaped occupied region growing from the bottom-left corner. States are monotone lattice paths, giving far fewer states than general skyline search, so L can reach about 20–24. This finds non-guillotine integer dissections, such as corner-heavy optima, exactly.</idea>

<idea>Insertion homotopy: start from the best layout for n−1, insert a zero-size square at every vertex where three or more squares meet or at a boundary corner gap. Grow that square continuously by re-solving the topology-fixed LP while its neighbours shrink, and keep the best final sum; repeat the analogous deletion path from the n+1 layout.</idea>

<idea>Precompute, by multi-start penalty optimisation with rotation, the best packings of m=2..6 squares in rectangles of aspect 1:1, 2:1, 3:2 and 3:1. Use them as tiles that replace equal-aspect blocks of grid cells, inserted through the existing replacement and knapsack machinery when their scaled (Δcount, Δsum) beats the axis-aligned retilings.</idea>

<idea>Row re-gridding with free count bumps: in a k-row layout, rows with k+j squares of side 1/(k+j) are always height-feasible alongside rows of k squares of side 1/k, and leave a residual horizontal strip of height Σ(1/k − 1/(k+j)). Enumerate row-count vectors and fill that residual strip with a row of tiny squares, plus LP compaction, to reach counts that neither the grid nor the Erdős–Soifer family reaches.</idea>

<idea>Unequal L-frame peeling: peel a frame along two adjacent edges whose squares are not all equal (for example one corner square of side a with runs of side b and c along the two arms). Choose a, b and c from small-denominator rationals so that both arms tile exactly, and recurse on the inner square. This generalises the n=11 frame construction beyond unit-fraction frames.</idea>

<idea>Contact-graph mining across n: take the best layouts found for neighbouring counts (n−2..n+2) and extract recurring local motifs, such as a 2×2-into-1 merge, an L-corner or a frame. Re-apply every motif at every compatible position of the current layout, scoring each result with the compaction LP, so improvements found at one n propagate to the others within the run.</idea>

<idea>Diagonal two-big-square family: place squares of sides a and 1−a in opposite corners, and fill the two off-diagonal a×(1−a) rectangles with the best rectangle-table packings using counts n1 and n2. Optimise a over rationals and also allow each big square to be subdivided into a j×j grid. This is a closed-form non-grid family that is cheap to enumerate.</idea>

<idea>Long shot on rotation: wherever a layout has a free square or near-square hole of side h, check whether a small square tilted at 45° plus axis-aligned slivers can increase the count with a smaller sum loss than an axis-aligned refill. Solve this as a tiny SLSQP inside the hole with the surrounding squares allowed to shrink linearly.</idea>

<idea>Random-restart integer perturbation: starting from the best layout expressed on an L×L board, apply random "slide a seam by one unit" moves that shift a maximal straight edge segment. Each move resizes the squares on both sides by ±1 unit, and the move is repaired by splitting or merging so the count stays n. Run thousands of exact-integer hill-climbing steps with occasional resets to the best.</idea>

<idea>Run simulated annealing over slicing floorplans written as normalized Polish expressions (operands are the n squares, operators H/V). Size each expression exactly with an LP that maximises the sum of sides, where each slice's width or height is shared and each leaf is constrained to be square. Use the standard Wong–Liu moves (swap adjacent operands, complement an operator chain, swap an operand with an operator). This explores guillotine layouts with continuous rather than discretised cut positions.</idea>

<idea>Treat the best count for a rectangle of aspect r as a piecewise-linear function g_m(r) and compute its breakpoints exactly in Fractions. Build it recursively from g for smaller counts by taking upper envelopes over the cut position. Optimal cuts can then sit at any rational breakpoint instead of only at denominators ≤ 12, and the unit square is just g_n(1).</idea>

<idea>Keep several layouts per count in the substitution/partition DP rather than only the max-sum one. Use a Pareto front on (sum, largest side) and also (sum, smallest side). A slightly worse layout with one big square is often the better host for later substitution or splitting steps. Prune dominated states only at the end.</idea>

<idea>Add an active-set rational reconstruction post-processor. After any continuous (SLSQP/penalty) optimisation, detect the near-active contacts (gap < 1e-7) and solve the resulting linear equality system exactly in Fractions to recover the exact rational optimum. Accept it if exact verification passes, so optimiser noise neither costs score nor causes invalid overlaps.</idea>

<idea>Use a first-order rigidity test to look for rotational improvements. For the best axis-aligned layout, linearise the separating-axis constraints in each square's translation, rotation and side-growth variables. Solve an LP asking for an infinitesimal motion that strictly increases the sum of sides while keeping all contacts feasible. If one exists, follow it with line search plus SLSQP, which shows exactly where tilting helps instead of guessing.</idea>

<idea>Test candidate multisets of sides for packability with Korf/Huang–Korf's two-phase rectangle-packing algorithm. First assign x-intervals with cumulative-width (wasted-space) pruning, then solve the y-placement as a separate CSP. Order squares in decreasing size and break symmetry by restricting the largest square to one quadrant. This is typically far faster than skyline backtracking, so many more knapsack multisets can be certified.</idea>

<idea>Use GRASP with path relinking on integer boards. Build many layouts by randomised greedy largest-fitting-square placement with random size caps, keep an elite pool per count, and walk between pairs of elite layouts by transferring sub-rectangle regions from one into the other. Repair the count by splitting or merging at each step, which recombines good local structures found in different runs.</idea>

<idea>Add a windmill motif as a replaceable block. Replace a 2×2 block of grid cells by four squares rotated by angle θ in pinwheel fashion around a fifth small central square, optimising θ and the sides numerically with exact separating-axis checks. Tabulate the motif's (Δcount=+1, Δsum) and also its 3×3 analogues, then feed them into the block-replacement knapsack as a rotated count-parity fix.</idea>

<idea>Place the refined Erdős–Soifer block at a non-aligned position: let the (m+1)×(m+1) fine grid straddle cell boundaries, offset by a fraction of a cell. Re-solve the neighbouring coarse cells with the compaction LP so partially covered cells become rectangles re-tiled by equal squares. This generates (Δcount, Δsum) pairs, including even count changes, that aligned replacements cannot give.</idea>

<idea>Build an "Egyptian-row" family. Stack horizontal rows where row i holds c_i squares of side 1/c_i, so each full row contributes exactly 1 to the sum and Σ1/c_i ≤ 1. Choose the vectors (c_i) by enumerating Egyptian-fraction decompositions with Σc_i close to n. Fill the leftover strip of height 1−Σ1/c_i with the transposed version of the same construction, recursing two levels, and zero-pad or delete to reach exactly n.</idea>

<idea>Build an exhaustive axis-aligned "count-sum" table T[p][q] over integer rectangles p×q (p,q ≤ 2√n+4), where each entry is a Pareto set of (count, sum) pairs. Fill it with exact-Fraction guillotine recursion that also allows the cell itself to be one square plus a remainder strip. Then return, for the unit square, the best entry at exactly n over all board sizes L, reconstructing the layout from stored back-pointers.</idea>

<idea>Add a "row-mixing" closed form. Use r rows: rows of the first kind hold a squares of side 1/a (height 1/a), and rows of the second kind hold b squares of side 1/b. Their heights must satisfy x/a + y/b ≤ 1. Enumerate integers a, b, x, y with xa + yb ≥ n, keep the largest sides when trimming, and maximise x + y minus the trimmed sides. Also fill any leftover strip with a final row of c squares of side min(leftover height, 1/c).</idea>

<idea>Implement the known optimal-pattern generator directly: for n = k² + 2m + 1 use Erdős–Soifer with the (m+1)×(m+1) refinement. For n = k² − 2m − 1 use the shrinking version, and for even residues combine one expanding and one shrinking replacement in disjoint corners of the same k-grid. Evaluate all (k, m1, m2) and validate with an exact Fraction overlap checker before returning.</idea>

<idea>Use a scipy-milp exact partition of an L×L integer board (L from ⌈√n⌉ to 3⌈√n⌉ within a time budget) into at most n axis-aligned integer squares. Binary variables x[i,j,s] place a square of side s at (i,j). Cover each cell at most once, require Σx = n, and maximise Σ s·x / L. Warm-start from the best closed-form answer and stop each L after a few seconds.</idea>

<idea>Use "deletion with re-expansion": take the k×k grid with k = ⌈√n⌉ and delete the k²−n surplus cells chosen as a whole row segment. Then merge the freed space with neighbouring cells into larger squares (e.g. delete 3 cells of a 2×2 corner and enlarge the 4th to side 2/k). Enumerate merge shapes j×j costing j²−1 deletions and gaining (j−1)/k each, which turns padding waste into sum.</idea>

<idea>Use a compaction LP with free sizes on a fixed slicing tree. For the best guillotine layout, set the leaf sides and cut positions as LP variables, constrained so that siblings share the parent's width or height, with sides ≤ the cell dimensions. Maximise the sum, then round the solution to exact rationals via active constraints. This rebalances strips that the discrete cut grid misallocated.</idea>

<idea>Run a SLSQP polish over all axis-aligned squares with the pairwise ordering fixed from the best construction (left/right/above/below per pair, chosen by the largest current separation). Use sides and centres as variables, so the solve is an LP. Then try flipping the ordering of each pair whose separation is tied, accepting improvements greedily within 20 seconds.</idea>

<idea>Long shot "tilted strip" family: take k−1 rows of a k-grid of side 1/k and replace the final row with a strip of height h, holding k+1 squares rotated by θ and touching alternately the top and bottom. Shrink the other rows to height (1−h)/(k−1). Solve the sum over (h, θ) numerically with exact rotated-square containment, accepting only when it beats the axis-aligned value for that n.</idea>

<idea>Recursive frame-peeling search. Choose a corner square of side 1−t, then fill the L-shaped border of width t with two arms of equal squares of side t/j (stacked j deep where possible). Recurse into any rectangle left over. Enumerate t ∈ {p/q : q ≤ 12} and depth ≤ 3, keeping the exact count n via the best (count, sum) Pareto lists of the sub-rectangles.</idea>

<idea>Run a bottom-left skyline beam search on an integer L×L board, where each step places at the lowest-left corner a square chosen from all sizes that fit. Score partial states by placed sum + √(remaining count × remaining area), which is the Cauchy–Schwarz bound. Use beam width ~500, iterate L over several values within the time limit, and return the best complete layout with exactly n squares.</idea>

<idea>Move every size-zero padding square off the interior. The current code puts them at (0.5,0.5), which lies inside a real square whenever k is odd, and a strict evaluator may count that as a shared interior point. Place them instead at distinct boundary corners or grid-line vertices, such as (0,0), (1,0) and points of the form (i/k, 0), which are never interior to any square.</idea>

<idea>Compute every coordinate from integer numerators, for example centre = (2i+1)/(2k) and side = p/q, evaluated once as a float. Then clamp centre ± side/2 into [0,1], and shrink each side by a relative 1e-13 only when a float check against the evaluator's likely tolerance fails. This removes accumulated rounding from repeated (i+0.5)*side products.</idea>

<idea>Build an exact monotone envelope F(n) = max over n' ≤ n of the expanding and shrinking Erdős–Soifer values k ± m/k (or (m+1)/k), each padded with zero squares. Pick, for each n, the realising layout with the fewest zero squares. A quick check shows this reproduces every listed best-known value (6→7/3, 7→5/2, 8→8/3, 11→13/4, 12→10/3, 13→7/2, 14→11/3, 15→15/4), and it also handles hidden n such as 18→4.2 and 20→4.4 through the shrinking branch of k+1.</idea>

<idea>Handle tiny and edge-case n explicitly but generically. For n=1 return the unit square. For n=2,3 compare 1 against splitting into halves (2×(1/2)=1, a tie). Make sure the k=1 and k=2 cases of the expand/shrink enumeration (for example n=4, and m=0 meaning no replacement) never index out of range or return fewer than n tuples.</idea>

<idea>Run a cross-entropy-method search over size multisets. Keep a probability vector over how many squares of each side 1/d (d ≤ 3√n) to use. Decode each sampled multiset with a skyline placer on the lcm board, keep the top 10% of samples that pack with exactly n squares, and re-estimate the distribution. This is a smoother alternative to the GA, seeded at the Erdős–Soifer multiset.</idea>

<idea>Long-shot self-similar family: tile a corner of the unit square with a geometric spiral of squares whose sides shrink by a ratio r (Fibonacci/golden-spiral or a rational approximation). Fill the complementary rectangle with the best uniform grid. Optimise r and the spiral length over rationals so that the total count is n, as a structurally non-lattice candidate.</idea>

<idea>Use the Erdős–Soifer layout as a seed for an angle-free/angle-on comparison. Add tiny random rotations (±0.5°) and position jitter to it, then run SLSQP maximising the sum under exact separating-axis constraints for about 20 s with multiple jitters. Return the rotated result only if it strictly exceeds the exact rational value by more than 1e-9.</idea>

<idea>Use an empty-cell two-level grid closed form: in a k1×k1 coarse grid, each cell is either one square, a j×j subgrid with a single global j, or left empty. With a full, b subdivided and e empty cells, count = a + b·j² and sum = (a + b·j)/k1. Enumerate (k1, j, a, b) over a + b + e = k1² to hit n exactly, without zero-padding waste.</idea>

<idea>Add an internal self-test run on the first call that evaluates solve(m) for m=1..40 using a strict exact-Fraction overlap and containment checker. Verify that the returned sum is non-decreasing in m and that each m has exactly m tuples; if any m violates this, substitute the best layout for a smaller m plus zero squares.</idea>

<idea>Choose the position of the refined (or coarsened) block to minimise floating-point risk, preferring the corner at the origin so that most coordinates are small exact dyadics or thirds. For two-block combinations, put the blocks in opposite corners. Before accepting, verify that their union does not exceed the k×k grid, so the combinatorial enumeration never emits overlapping replacements.</idea>

<idea>Run an exact branch-and-bound over integer square dissections of a k×k board (k = ⌈√n⌉ … ⌈√n⌉+3). Enumerate only "grid plus a single non-unit square of side a placed at a corner, with the cells covered by it removed", and also the dual case where cells are split into 2×2. Take the best exact count n, as a fast closed-form family indexed by (k, a, number of 2×2 splits).</idea>

<idea>Generalise the one-sided L-frame recursion to "corner square plus a two-arm frame of side 1/j". The bottom arm holds j squares of side 1/j and the left arm holds j−1 of them. The remaining (1−1/j)×(1−1/j) square is filled recursively, scaled from best[m], with the table built bottom-up. Evaluate f(n) ≥ (2j−1)/j + (1−1/j)·f(n−2j+1) for all j.</idea>

<idea>Add a "rectangle-of-two-grids" closed form. Split the square vertically at x = p/(p+q)-type rationals. Fill the left part with an a×b grid of equal squares and the right part with a c×d grid, with the sides chosen as the min of the width and height constraints. Enumerate all integer tuples with total count ≥ n, trim the smallest squares, and keep the best exact value.</idea>

<idea>Implement the Pareto-front substitution DP restricted to the four corner sub-squares. Split the unit square into one sub-square of side t and the L-shaped complement, decomposed into two rectangles. Each rectangle uses its best uniform grid, t ranges over rationals p/q with q ≤ 2√n+2, and the count is matched exactly by combining the per-rectangle count/sum lists.</idea>

<idea>As a correctness safeguard, compute all candidate configurations in Fractions. Before converting to floats, run an exact pairwise interval-overlap check and an exact containment check. Place zero-size padding squares at the corner (0,0) rather than the centre, so the evaluator never flags a point inside another square's interior.</idea>

<idea>Implement the strip-mixing form directly. Use x rows of a squares of side 1/a and y rows of a+1 squares of side 1/(a+1), with x/a + y/(a+1) ≤ 1, then put a final leftover row of c squares in the residual height. Enumerate a, x, y and c, which naturally yields values like (k·j + b)/j that match the best-known pattern for even n.</idea>

<idea>Run a small exact integer-board DP (a skyline or profile DP on an L×L board, L ≤ 10, with square sides 1..L). The DP tracks the best sum for every count, so the true optimal axis-aligned integer dissection is found for small n. Prune it with a time cap and keep it as one of the candidates.</idea>

<idea>Long shot: start from the best rational layout and remove the smallest square, opening a hole. Then run penalty-based SLSQP with rotations allowed only for the squares neighbouring that hole, and look for a tilted re-arrangement that fits n squares with a larger total. Accept the result only after an exact separating-axis verification passes with margin.</idea>

<idea>Add a Lagrangian-hull rescue for every n. Compute the upper concave hull of (count, best sum) over all constructions found, for counts from n−6 to n+6. For any n strictly below the hull, try combining the two hull endpoints' layouts by placing them as scaled sub-blocks in a 2×1 or 1×2 split. Use the best sub-layouts for the rectangles via the rectangle table.</idea>

<idea>Use a "staircase merge" family on the k×k grid with k = ⌈√n⌉+1. Merge disjoint 2×2 blocks along the diagonal into single squares of side 2/k, each removing 3 from the count and adding 1/k to the sum. Also allow 3×3 merges, each removing 8 and adding 2/k, and choose the counts by a small knapsack to hit n exactly with the maximal sum.</idea>

ideas.text: Implement the Erdős–Soifer family directly: for each k, start from the k×k grid of cells of side 1/k and replace one m×m block of cells by an (m+1)×(m+1) grid of squares of side m/((m+1)k). This adds 2m+1 squares and m/k to the total, so n = k²+2m+1 gives k + m/k. Evaluate every feasible (k, m) for the given n, pad any surplus with size-zero squares, and keep the best.

Add the shrinking variant to the same search: replace an (m+1)×(m+1) block of cells by an m×m grid of squares of side (m+1)/(mk). This removes 2m+1 squares at a cost of (m+1)/k, so a larger k can be used when n sits just below a perfect square (e.g. n=6, 8, 11, 13, 15). Take the maximum over both variants and all k.

Generalise to multiple disjoint block replacements inside one k×k grid, with different block sizes and either direction. Solve a small knapsack over (count change, sum change) pairs to hit exactly n squares with maximal total, padding with zero squares only if needed.

Allow the replaced block to be a rectangle: an a×b block of cells, re-tiled by p×q equal squares of side min(a/p, b/q)/k. Enumerate all small a, b, p, q to find count/sum trade-offs the square-block construction misses. This matters especially for even n, where single square-block changes only shift the count by odd amounts.

Use non-uniform grids: choose row heights h_i and column widths w_j and put a square of side min(h_i, w_j) in each cell. Optimise these sizes with an LP or SLSQP, together with subdivided cells, to maximise the sum for awkward n. Seed the optimisation from the best Erdős–Soifer configuration.

Recursive guillotine dynamic programming: f(rectangle a×b, count n) = best of placing a single square or making a vertical/horizontal cut and splitting n between the parts. Run it over a discretised set of rectangle dimensions, e.g. multiples of 1/(k·L), to discover axis-aligned packings better than the formula.

Build the configuration from a staircase/L-shaped strip: keep a (k−1)×(k−1) grid of side 1/k in one corner. Fill the remaining L-shaped strip of width 1/k with squares of side 1/(k+j) or smaller, chosen so the count and sum work out; this gives intermediate n values between the block-replacement constructions.

As a long shot for rotated squares, place 45°-rotated small squares into gaps left by an axis-aligned grid whose cells are slightly shrunk. Use penalty-based gradient optimisation (separating-axis overlap penalty plus containment penalty) to maximise the sum, starting from the best constructive answer.

Add a robust validation-and-shrink step: compute exact coordinates with rationals or Fractions, then scale every side by (1−1e-12) about its centre. This ensures no floating-point overlap or out-of-bounds error loses points in the evaluator, while costing a negligible amount of score.

Run a fast local search over discrete configurations (grid parameter k, block positions and sizes, and which squares to merge or split) using a simulated-annealing loop for a few seconds. Score each candidate with the exact sum-of-sides formula and return the best valid packing found.

Safe baseline fix: for each n, also try k = ceil(sqrt(n)) and use n cells of the k×k grid with side 1/k, giving n/k. This alone matches the best known values for n=8 and n=15. Return the maximum of this and every other construction found.

Represent axis-aligned packings as sequence pairs, which fix for each pair of squares whether one is left of or below the other. For a fixed sequence pair, maximise the sum of sides with an exact LP whose variables are the positions and sides, using linear separation and containment constraints. Search over sequence pairs with simulated annealing, seeded from the best grid-based construction, until the time budget runs out.

Exact tiling search on an integer L×L board for L up to about 10–12. Use a broken-profile (skyline) DP or exact-cover backtracking to enumerate dissections of the board into integer squares, recording the best total of sides per count. Scale by 1/L, and pad or drop cells (as zero squares) to hit n exactly.

Use an ILP or set-partitioning solver, such as scipy milp, on a k×k cell grid. Each candidate is an a×a axis-aligned block at any position, chosen with a binary variable; constraints are that each cell is covered at most once and that the number of squares chosen equals n. Maximise the sum of a/k, and loop over k from about sqrt(n)−2 to 2·sqrt(n).

Dynamic program over multisets of square sizes. Moves are splitting a square of side s into j×j squares of side s/j (adding j²−1 squares and gaining (j−1)s), or merging an aligned j×j group back into one. Run best-first search from every k×k grid to fill a table best[n] and its realising layout, keeping the geometry as an explicit quadtree-like tree.

Column-strip construction: split the unit square into vertical strips of widths w_i, and stack c_i equal squares of side min(w_i, 1/c_i) in each strip. Each strip may also be recursively split horizontally into sub-strips. Optimise the integers c_i by DP, setting the widths to w_i = 1/c_i where possible and giving any leftover width to a final strip, to cover counts the square-grid families miss.

Two-scale mixed lattice: tile the square with a p×p grid in which some cells hold one square of side 1/p and others hold a q×q subgrid. Allow p and q to be coprime-unrelated, and let the subdivided region be a whole band of rows so that the band is re-gridded with a different column count. Enumerate p, q, the band heights and counts in closed form.

Gap-filling post-processor: after any construction, compute the free space as a union of axis-aligned empty rectangles, using maximal-rectangle enumeration. Repeatedly replace a zero-size padding square with the largest square that fits a free rectangle, and enlarge existing squares into adjacent slack using an LP over sides with positions free.

Tilted-band long shot: lay out the k×k grid but replace one row (or column) with k+1 squares rotated by a small angle θ, stacked as a tilted chain in a strip of height slightly above 1/k. Shrink the other rows accordingly, then optimise θ, the strip height and the side lengths numerically with exact separating-axis feasibility checks. This targets n = k²+1-type values where a lattice cannot fit the extra square.

Recursive “one big square plus two rectangles” construction: put a square of side s in a corner and split the remaining L-shape into two rectangles. Fill each rectangle optimally by a memoised recursion on (aspect ratio, count), where a rectangle a×b with count m is filled by a grid of ⌊b/a⌋-style columns or recursion. Optimise s over a fine set of rationals.

Substitution DP: any square of side s in a packing can be replaced by a scaled copy of a packing of m squares, so f(n+m−1) ≥ f(n) − s + s·f(m). Fill a table best[n] bottom-up from the k×k grids, keeping each layout as an explicit tree. At each step substitute into either the largest or the smallest square, and try every m that has already been solved.

Over-build then delete: build Erdős–Soifer or grid configurations for every N in n..n+2√n+2 and delete the N−n smallest squares. This gives f(n) ≥ f(N) − (sum of the N−n smallest sides). Add every such candidate to the pool and keep the best one that is valid.

Multiset-first packing: enumerate multisets of sides from {1/d} (d up to about 3√n) by a knapsack. Maximise the sum subject to the count being n and the area being at most 1, then test the top candidates for exact packability. The test is a bottom-left/skyline backtracking search on the integer board of size lcm(d's) × lcm(d's), returning the first multiset that packs.

Exact axis-aligned optimum for small n via a big-M MILP in scipy.optimize.milp. Use continuous centres and sides, and four binary separation indicators per pair (left/right/below/above, at least one active). Add symmetry breaking (sort by side, put the first square in the bottom-left quadrant) and warm-start from the best construction.

Inflation multi-start for rotated packings: start from many random centres, angles and tiny sides. Run a Lubachevsky–Stillinger-style growth in which each square's side grows at a rate proportional to its slack. Resolve overlaps with separating-axis push-apart moves plus rotation, then run a final SLSQP polish on sum(sides) with exact separating-axis constraints.

Symmetry-constrained continuous search: impose mirror or 180°-rotational symmetry (with an odd central square when n is odd). This halves the variables in the penalty/SLSQP optimisation of rotated squares and lets many more restarts fit in 60 s, exploring structures such as a central tilted square surrounded by symmetric axis-aligned rings.

Pythagorean-tiling candidate: tile the plane with two square sizes a and b in the Pythagorean (pinwheel) arrangement, optionally rotated by a small angle. Clip it to the unit square, keeping only squares that lie fully inside and zero-padding. Optimise a, b, the offset and the angle numerically to see whether the two-size lattice beats grid families for some n.

Beam-search greedy placement: compute the largest empty axis-aligned square in the current free region (L∞-Voronoi / maximal empty square). At each step choose among a few candidate sizes at the top candidate positions, scoring partial states by sum + (remaining count)·(average feasible future side). Keep a beam of 50–200 states.

Tilted-lattice core with axis-aligned border: place a k×k block of squares rotated by a Pythagorean angle such as atan(1/2) or atan(3/4) in the middle. Fill the four triangular-ish border regions with axis-aligned small squares from the guillotine/strip routines. Optimise the lattice side and angle so the total count is n, as a long shot for n just above a perfect square.

Nested two-level Erdős–Soifer closed form: inside the (m+1)×(m+1) replacement grid, apply a second replacement of an m2×m2 block by (m2±1)² squares. This gives counts k² + 2m+1 ± (2m2±1) with explicit sums. Enumerate all (k, m, m2, signs, positions) and take the best that exactly matches n.

Ring recursion: surround a central square of side 1−2a with a frame of 4(j−1) squares of side a=1/j along all four edges. Fill the central square recursively with the best scaled packing for the remaining count, and enumerate j and the recursion depth. One-sided L-frames already give n=6 (7/3) and n=11 (3/4 frame of 7 plus four squares of 3/8, totalling 3.25), and this generalises them to two- and four-sided frames.

Exact rectangle table g(p,q,m): for integer rectangles p×q up to about 12 and counts m up to n, store the best sum from a single square, a uniform grid, or one guillotine cut. Compute it with memoised DP in exact Fractions. The unit square is then filled by trying every split of the 1×1 board at rational cut positions with denominators up to 12, which captures nested L-shapes and asymmetric cuts in one table.

Hole-punch post-optimiser: take the best construction, pick the r smallest squares (r=1..4), delete them, and compute every maximal empty axis-aligned rectangle of the freed region. Refill it with the best g(rectangle, r') packing from the rectangle table, keeping the result if it beats the original at the same count n.

Compaction LP on the topology of the best construction: freeze only the left/right/above/below contact relations between squares. Solve an LP maximising the sum of sides under those relations and containment; this often lets unequal neighbours rebalance, for example growing a big corner square while shrinking a strip. Accept the result only if it is strictly larger.

Two-band construction with unequal frame widths: give the bottom band height a with ⌊1/a⌋ squares and the left band width b with ⌊(1−a)/b⌋ squares, where a and b are independent unit fractions. Fill the remaining (1−b)×(1−a) rectangle with the best grid of near-square cells. Enumerate a and b over 1/2..1/(2√n) and the inner grid shape, in closed form.

Geometric staircase along the diagonal: place squares of decreasing sides s1>s2>… along the main diagonal. Fill the two triangular-ish complementary staircase regions with column and row stacks whose sizes are matched to the step heights. Optimise the s_i with SLSQP for each n as a structurally different, non-grid family.

Upper-bound-pruned exhaustive search for small n (≤20): enumerate axis-aligned dissections in bottom-left skyline order with side choices from {i/L : L≤12}. Prune with the Cauchy–Schwarz bound sum ≤ current + √(m·remaining area) and with the best known lower bound, so the exact discrete optimum is found within the time limit.

Rotated-insert perturbation: in the best axis-aligned configuration, find pairs of adjacent equal squares in a strip whose width has slack, and replace a run of t squares by t+1 squares tilted at angle θ. Solve the 1-D chain-in-strip problem (side as a function of θ and strip width) in closed form and accept the change when the count-adjusted sum improves.

Count-parity fix via 2×1 dominos: replace a 1×2 block of cells of side 1/k by three squares (one of side 1/k... rather two of side 1/(2k) stacked plus one of 1/k), or 2×3 blocks by six cells' worth of mixed sizes. Tabulate every small rectangular block retiling with (Δcount, Δsum) from the exact rectangle table, then knapsack these onto disjoint regions of the k×k grid to hit even n exactly.

Safety-first output: build every candidate in exact Fractions, validate it with an exact axis-aligned overlap and containment checker (separating axis with an epsilon for any rotated ones), and shrink sides by 1e-12 only if needed. If the top candidate fails, fall back to the next valid candidate, so no n ever scores below the plain ceil(√n) grid value n/⌈√n⌉.

Add a partition recurrence: split the unit square into a j×j grid of equal sub-squares (j=2,3,4) and give each sub-square its own count n_i with Σn_i = n. This gives f(n) ≥ (1/j)·max Σ f(n_i), computed by a knapsack over a best[] table built bottom-up. Unlike single-square substitution, the extra count is spread over all cells, which reaches mixed-parity counts.

Generate perfect and imperfect squared rectangles via Brooks–Smith–Stone–Tutte electrical networks. Enumerate small planar graphs (up to about n+3 edges), solve Kirchhoff's equations exactly with Fractions to get square dissections of a square with exactly n tiles, and take the best sum. Near-square rectangle dissections are also kept, scaled into the unit square with the leftover strip filled by zero-size or small squares.

Use a genetic/decoder approach. A chromosome is an ordered list of n sides drawn from {1/d}, and a deterministic skyline (bottom-left-fill) decoder places them and sets any square that does not fit to zero. Evolve multisets and orderings with crossover and mutation for ~40 s, seeded from the grid and Erdős–Soifer multisets.

Use non-guillotine pinwheel decompositions. Split the unit square into four rectangles spiralling around a central rectangle, with the cut positions enumerated over rationals of denominator ≤ 12. Fill each of the five rectangles from an exact rectangle-count table, which captures layouts no sequence of straight cuts can reach.

Compute a global table best[m] with its layouts once per process, for all m up to max(n) + 2√n, stored in a module-level cache. Every construction family (grids, replacements, partitions, substitutions) can then feed the others, and repeated calls cost nothing. This leaves most of the 60 s budget for numerical refinement of only the current n.

Implement the known upper bounds as an early exit and a search guide. These are f(k²) = k (Erdős), the bound f(k²+1) ≤ k for k ≤ 13 (Halbeisen), and the Cauchy–Schwarz bound √n. When a candidate meets the bound, return immediately; otherwise spend the remaining time on the n with the largest gap between candidate and bound.

Seam construction with tilted squares: put a k-column grid on the left part of the square and a (k+1)-column grid on the right, with different row pitches. Along the vertical seam where the pitches mismatch, insert a column of slightly rotated squares. Optimise the seam position, the angles and the sides with SLSQP using exact separating-axis constraints, so that counts between the two lattices fill naturally.

Column generation for strip-based packings. Each column pattern is a vertical strip of width w holding a mixed stack, such as one square of side w plus pairs of side w/2 side by side. Solve the master LP "choose strips with total width ≤ 1 and exact count n, maximising the sum", price new strip patterns by DP, then round to integers.

Shift-and-squeeze brick rows: lay out rows of equal squares in which consecutive rows are offset by half a cell. Shrink a few rows so that one row can host an extra square of a different size in the freed gap. Optimise the row heights and offsets by LP for fixed integer row counts, enumerating row-count vectors whose total is n.

Large-neighbourhood search on the best axis-aligned layout. Repeatedly free a random window (for example a 2×2 to 4×4 region of cells), then solve the window exactly. The exact solve maximises the sum of sides inside the window's bounding box with a fixed count, using the small big-M MILP or a brute-force integer tiling. Accept improvements and cycle through windows and counts until the time limit.

Continuous two-rectangle split: cut the unit square at height t into a 1×t and a 1×(1−t) rectangle and fill each with a uniform p×q (resp. p'×q') grid of side min(t/p, 1/q) (resp. min((1−t)/p', 1/q')). For every integer tuple with pq+p'q' ≥ n, solve analytically for the optimal t (a breakpoint of piecewise-linear functions), then recurse one level on the larger part.

Euclidean-algorithm squared rectangles: for a rational aspect a/b, greedily cut the largest possible square from the remaining rectangle (the continued-fraction dissection). Place such a rectangle in the unit square, fill the complementary strip with a grid, and subdivide individual pieces into j×j grids. Enumerate a/b with small denominators to hit count n with the maximal sum.

Use OR-Tools CP-SAT, if importable, with optional 2D intervals (AddNoOverlap2D) on an integer L×L board. Each candidate square has a size variable chosen from a domain, presence literals are constrained to sum to n, and the objective is the total of the sides. Iterate L over 6..16 with time slices and fall back to the closed-form constructions if the library is absent.

Three-level nested shelves: rows inside columns inside rows. Each shelf has an integer count c, and its height equals the shelf's square side. Shelves stack until the leftover, which is filled by a transposed shelf system, recursively to depth 3. Enumerate the count vectors by DP over the remaining (width, height, count) state, using exact Fractions.

Size-class realisability search: fix 2–3 size classes with counts (n1, n2, n3) and sides (s1, s2, s3) tied by small integer ratios. Maximise Σ n_i s_i subject to the area constraint and a strip-packing necessary condition: the number of columns of the largest class times s1 must be ≤ 1. Then construct the layout explicitly by placing the big class as a corner block and greedily tiling the L-shaped remainder with the smaller classes.

Pattern mining from the best-known values: all listed optima have the form (k² + a)/k or (k·j + b)/j with small integers. Generate every rational of this form near √n, and for each target rebuild a matching layout by bounded backtracking on the corresponding k×k or j×j integer board. A target therefore steers an exact search instead of blind enumeration.

Two-orientation hybrid in one block: replace an m×m block of cells by a 45°-rotated grid of diamonds of side s. Fill the four corner triangles of that block with axis-aligned staircases of tiny squares. Choose s and the diamond count analytically so the block gains count at a sum cost below the Erdős–Soifer replacement's, then insert the block via the existing knapsack.

Parallel portfolio: run independent construction families (closed forms, guillotine DP, MILP/CP, continuous rotated optimisation) in separate multiprocessing workers with hard deadlines of about 50 s. A shared best-so-far value prunes all of them. The parent validates and returns the best certified packing, so slow exact searches never risk the time limit.

Contact-graph flipping search: represent the axis-aligned packing by its horizontal and vertical constraint graphs. Make local moves that flip one adjacency (left-of becomes below-of) or merge or split a node, re-solving the sum-maximising LP after each move with warm-started dual simplex. This is a cheaper neighbourhood than full sequence pairs and lets tabu search explore thousands of topologies per second.

Asymmetric corner-merge family: in a k×k grid, merge an a×a block in one corner and a b×b block in the opposite corner (with a ≠ b allowed). Also split c cells into 2×2, giving count k² − a² − b² + 2 + 3c and sum k + (a + b − a² − b² + c)/k... wait, corrected: (k² − a² − b² + a + b + c)/k. Enumerate all (k, a, b, c) in closed form to cover even and odd residues near n that single-block replacements miss.

Solve a maximum-weight independent set ILP on a mixed-denominator lattice. Candidate axis-aligned squares have sides i/L and corners on an L×L board with highly composite L (12, 24 or 60), so sizes like 1/3, 1/4 and 3/8 coexist. Non-overlap is enforced by a clique constraint at every interior lattice point, plus an exact count of n.

Run Monte Carlo Tree Search over bottom-left skyline placements. Each move picks the side of the next square at the lowest-leftmost skyline corner from a small set of rational sizes, and rollouts finish greedily, with the remaining squares counted at their best feasible equal size. Use UCT statistics shared through a transposition table keyed on the skyline profile.

Use objective continuation in the continuous optimiser: maximise Σ s_i^p, starting at p=2, where many equal-area tilings are optimal and the landscape is flat. Gradually anneal p down to 1 while keeping the separating-axis and containment constraints, so the optimiser is led from tiling-like configurations towards sum-of-sides optima, possibly rotated ones.

Run an L∞ power-diagram (Laguerre–Chebyshev) Lloyd relaxation. Give each of the n sites a weight, compute the L∞ power cells in the unit square, and set each square to the largest axis-aligned square centred in its cell. Iterate moving sites to the cell's Chebyshev centre and rebalancing weights towards equal-side growth.

Evolve construction expressions with grammar-based genetic programming. The primitives are grid(p,q), cut(h|v, t, A, B), split(j), merge(j) and ring(j, A), applied to a rectangle. Expressions are evaluated exactly in Fractions to get (count, sum), and the fitness is the best sum at exactly n with zero-padding, so new compositional families are discovered automatically.

Build a sheared staircase grid. Shift row i of a k×k-style grid horizontally by i·δ, which opens a staircase of left-edge gaps of widths δ, 2δ, …. Fill those gaps with squares of side iδ (or stacks of smaller ones), shrinking the row squares by LP, and enumerate k and rational δ in closed form to obtain extra counts at small sum cost.

Use LP dual sensitivity to guide splitting. Solve the compaction LP for the current best layout, read the dual prices of the containment and adjacency constraints, and split, merge or delete the squares with the most favourable marginal value per unit count change. Re-solve after each edit, which gives a targeted descent across counts n±1, n±3 instead of random moves.

Filter knapsack-generated multisets with necessary cumulative-capacity conditions before running the expensive packability tests. The number of squares with side > 1/j is at most (j−1)², and the total side of squares exceeding 1/2 in any row band is at most 1. Also apply an area bound per size threshold, so only plausible multisets reach exact packing.

Use tilted equal-square packings as sub-blocks. Precompute, by penalty optimisation, small near-optimal rotated packings of m equal squares in a square container (Friedman-type, e.g. m=5, 10, 11). Treat each as a substitutable block with its (count, scaled sum) in the substitution and partition recurrences, so rotated structures can appear inside otherwise axis-aligned layouts.

Use row-slide insertion moves. In the best layout, find a maximal straight line of edges spanning the square (a guillotine seam) and slide everything on one side by δ to open a strip. Fill the strip with a column of equal small squares, then re-solve the compaction LP so neighbours absorb the loss. Choose δ analytically as the breakpoint where the added count's sum exceeds the shrinkage cost.

Lagrangian count pricing: for a range of prices λ, maximise (sum of sides − λ·count) over guillotine/grid-tree layouts with a DP that never fixes the count. Each λ yields a layout on the upper convex hull of (count, sum). Then repair the count to exactly n with the cheapest local split, merge or delete, which finds good counts without enumerating every count.

Monotone-staircase DP: on an L×L integer board, restrict layouts to those built by placing squares into the inner corners of a Young-diagram-shaped occupied region growing from the bottom-left corner. States are monotone lattice paths, giving far fewer states than general skyline search, so L can reach about 20–24. This finds non-guillotine integer dissections, such as corner-heavy optima, exactly.

Insertion homotopy: start from the best layout for n−1, insert a zero-size square at every vertex where three or more squares meet or at a boundary corner gap. Grow that square continuously by re-solving the topology-fixed LP while its neighbours shrink, and keep the best final sum; repeat the analogous deletion path from the n+1 layout.

Precompute, by multi-start penalty optimisation with rotation, the best packings of m=2..6 squares in rectangles of aspect 1:1, 2:1, 3:2 and 3:1. Use them as tiles that replace equal-aspect blocks of grid cells, inserted through the existing replacement and knapsack machinery when their scaled (Δcount, Δsum) beats the axis-aligned retilings.

Row re-gridding with free count bumps: in a k-row layout, rows with k+j squares of side 1/(k+j) are always height-feasible alongside rows of k squares of side 1/k, and leave a residual horizontal strip of height Σ(1/k − 1/(k+j)). Enumerate row-count vectors and fill that residual strip with a row of tiny squares, plus LP compaction, to reach counts that neither the grid nor the Erdős–Soifer family reaches.

Unequal L-frame peeling: peel a frame along two adjacent edges whose squares are not all equal (for example one corner square of side a with runs of side b and c along the two arms). Choose a, b and c from small-denominator rationals so that both arms tile exactly, and recurse on the inner square. This generalises the n=11 frame construction beyond unit-fraction frames.

Contact-graph mining across n: take the best layouts found for neighbouring counts (n−2..n+2) and extract recurring local motifs, such as a 2×2-into-1 merge, an L-corner or a frame. Re-apply every motif at every compatible position of the current layout, scoring each result with the compaction LP, so improvements found at one n propagate to the others within the run.

Diagonal two-big-square family: place squares of sides a and 1−a in opposite corners, and fill the two off-diagonal a×(1−a) rectangles with the best rectangle-table packings using counts n1 and n2. Optimise a over rationals and also allow each big square to be subdivided into a j×j grid. This is a closed-form non-grid family that is cheap to enumerate.

Long shot on rotation: wherever a layout has a free square or near-square hole of side h, check whether a small square tilted at 45° plus axis-aligned slivers can increase the count with a smaller sum loss than an axis-aligned refill. Solve this as a tiny SLSQP inside the hole with the surrounding squares allowed to shrink linearly.

Random-restart integer perturbation: starting from the best layout expressed on an L×L board, apply random "slide a seam by one unit" moves that shift a maximal straight edge segment. Each move resizes the squares on both sides by ±1 unit, and the move is repaired by splitting or merging so the count stays n. Run thousands of exact-integer hill-climbing steps with occasional resets to the best.

Run simulated annealing over slicing floorplans written as normalized Polish expressions (operands are the n squares, operators H/V). Size each expression exactly with an LP that maximises the sum of sides, where each slice's width or height is shared and each leaf is constrained to be square. Use the standard Wong–Liu moves (swap adjacent operands, complement an operator chain, swap an operand with an operator). This explores guillotine layouts with continuous rather than discretised cut positions.

Treat the best count for a rectangle of aspect r as a piecewise-linear function g_m(r) and compute its breakpoints exactly in Fractions. Build it recursively from g for smaller counts by taking upper envelopes over the cut position. Optimal cuts can then sit at any rational breakpoint instead of only at denominators ≤ 12, and the unit square is just g_n(1).

Keep several layouts per count in the substitution/partition DP rather than only the max-sum one. Use a Pareto front on (sum, largest side) and also (sum, smallest side). A slightly worse layout with one big square is often the better host for later substitution or splitting steps. Prune dominated states only at the end.

Add an active-set rational reconstruction post-processor. After any continuous (SLSQP/penalty) optimisation, detect the near-active contacts (gap < 1e-7) and solve the resulting linear equality system exactly in Fractions to recover the exact rational optimum. Accept it if exact verification passes, so optimiser noise neither costs score nor causes invalid overlaps.

Use a first-order rigidity test to look for rotational improvements. For the best axis-aligned layout, linearise the separating-axis constraints in each square's translation, rotation and side-growth variables. Solve an LP asking for an infinitesimal motion that strictly increases the sum of sides while keeping all contacts feasible. If one exists, follow it with line search plus SLSQP, which shows exactly where tilting helps instead of guessing.

Test candidate multisets of sides for packability with Korf/Huang–Korf's two-phase rectangle-packing algorithm. First assign x-intervals with cumulative-width (wasted-space) pruning, then solve the y-placement as a separate CSP. Order squares in decreasing size and break symmetry by restricting the largest square to one quadrant. This is typically far faster than skyline backtracking, so many more knapsack multisets can be certified.

Use GRASP with path relinking on integer boards. Build many layouts by randomised greedy largest-fitting-square placement with random size caps, keep an elite pool per count, and walk between pairs of elite layouts by transferring sub-rectangle regions from one into the other. Repair the count by splitting or merging at each step, which recombines good local structures found in different runs.

Add a windmill motif as a replaceable block. Replace a 2×2 block of grid cells by four squares rotated by angle θ in pinwheel fashion around a fifth small central square, optimising θ and the sides numerically with exact separating-axis checks. Tabulate the motif's (Δcount=+1, Δsum) and also its 3×3 analogues, then feed them into the block-replacement knapsack as a rotated count-parity fix.

Place the refined Erdős–Soifer block at a non-aligned position: let the (m+1)×(m+1) fine grid straddle cell boundaries, offset by a fraction of a cell. Re-solve the neighbouring coarse cells with the compaction LP so partially covered cells become rectangles re-tiled by equal squares. This generates (Δcount, Δsum) pairs, including even count changes, that aligned replacements cannot give.

Build an "Egyptian-row" family. Stack horizontal rows where row i holds c_i squares of side 1/c_i, so each full row contributes exactly 1 to the sum and Σ1/c_i ≤ 1. Choose the vectors (c_i) by enumerating Egyptian-fraction decompositions with Σc_i close to n. Fill the leftover strip of height 1−Σ1/c_i with the transposed version of the same construction, recursing two levels, and zero-pad or delete to reach exactly n.

Build an exhaustive axis-aligned "count-sum" table T[p][q] over integer rectangles p×q (p,q ≤ 2√n+4), where each entry is a Pareto set of (count, sum) pairs. Fill it with exact-Fraction guillotine recursion that also allows the cell itself to be one square plus a remainder strip. Then return, for the unit square, the best entry at exactly n over all board sizes L, reconstructing the layout from stored back-pointers.

Add a "row-mixing" closed form. Use r rows: rows of the first kind hold a squares of side 1/a (height 1/a), and rows of the second kind hold b squares of side 1/b. Their heights must satisfy x/a + y/b ≤ 1. Enumerate integers a, b, x, y with xa + yb ≥ n, keep the largest sides when trimming, and maximise x + y minus the trimmed sides. Also fill any leftover strip with a final row of c squares of side min(leftover height, 1/c).

Implement the known optimal-pattern generator directly: for n = k² + 2m + 1 use Erdős–Soifer with the (m+1)×(m+1) refinement. For n = k² − 2m − 1 use the shrinking version, and for even residues combine one expanding and one shrinking replacement in disjoint corners of the same k-grid. Evaluate all (k, m1, m2) and validate with an exact Fraction overlap checker before returning.

Use a scipy-milp exact partition of an L×L integer board (L from ⌈√n⌉ to 3⌈√n⌉ within a time budget) into at most n axis-aligned integer squares. Binary variables x[i,j,s] place a square of side s at (i,j). Cover each cell at most once, require Σx = n, and maximise Σ s·x / L. Warm-start from the best closed-form answer and stop each L after a few seconds.

Use "deletion with re-expansion": take the k×k grid with k = ⌈√n⌉ and delete the k²−n surplus cells chosen as a whole row segment. Then merge the freed space with neighbouring cells into larger squares (e.g. delete 3 cells of a 2×2 corner and enlarge the 4th to side 2/k). Enumerate merge shapes j×j costing j²−1 deletions and gaining (j−1)/k each, which turns padding waste into sum.

Use a compaction LP with free sizes on a fixed slicing tree. For the best guillotine layout, set the leaf sides and cut positions as LP variables, constrained so that siblings share the parent's width or height, with sides ≤ the cell dimensions.
